scope_note: A sourced comparison of wake-word and keyword-spotting engines -- "how do I make a device listen for one phrase without running a full ASR pipeline 24/7." Covers open-source engines you self-host and commercial SDKs with vendor-fixed or trainable custom wake phrases. This project runs no false-accept/false-reject benchmarks of its own; accuracy figures are attributed and marked accordingly.
method_note: Every claim is checked against the vendor's own documentation or source repository before publication, then adversarially audited in a second pass that actively tries to refute each field rather than confirm it, followed by a dedicated facet-recheck pass verifying every facet against the row's own (possibly-corrected) text. Custom-wake-word claims are checked specifically for licensing restrictions on commercial use, not just technical capability.

systems.name: openWakeWord
systems.price_note: Free, self-hosted — no account, no cloud call
systems.method: Streaming classifier on top of a shared Google speech-embedding model: 80ms audio frames -> pretrained embedding -> lightweight per-wakeword classification head, run locally via ONNX Runtime or TFLite with no cloud round-trip.
systems.availability: Open source, pip-installable (`pip install openwakeword`); runs on Linux/Windows/macOS/Raspberry Pi; ships 6 pretrained wake words (alexa, hey mycroft, hey jarvis, hey rhasspy, timer, weather) plus a Colab-notebook pipeline to train your own.
systems.best_for: Local voice projects (Home Assistant, ESPHome, Wyoming-based setups) that want a ready CPU-only wake word with an accessible custom-training path, where the builder is prepared to either train their own model or clear the non-commercial model licence before shipping commercially.
systems.watch: The Apache-2.0 code and the actual pretrained models it ships sit under two different licences: the models are CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (non-commercial) because of their training-data provenance, so a product that ships the maintainer's default 'alexa'/'hey jarvis' models commercially is out of licence. The fix is training your own model with the same open pipeline, not swapping engines.
systems.standout: The only engine here with a genuinely turnkey custom-training path — a Colab notebook using synthetic Piper-TTS speech plus a large negative-audio corpus, runnable in under an hour by a non-ML-engineer — which is why it has become the de facto default across the Home Assistant / ESPHome / Wyoming ecosystem.
systems.accuracy_note: Maintainer-published target of under 5% false-reject rate and under 0.5 false-accepts/hour on the bundled reference models, with the 'alexa' model reported by the maintainer to outperform Picovoice Porcupine's equivalent on the same test clips; not independently re-verified.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — open pipeline using synthetic TTS-generated speech plus a large negative-audio corpus, packaged as a Colab notebook; no vendor account or paid step required.
systems.footprint: CPU-only; maintainer reports a single core of a Raspberry Pi 3 can run 15-20 openWakeWord models concurrently.
systems.adoption: Bundled/default wake-word engine for Home Assistant's voice stack (the official openWakeWord Home Assistant OS add-on, integrated via the Wyoming protocol) and widely used across ESPHome and Wyoming-protocol voice-satellite projects. Note: Home Assistant's own Voice Preview Edition (Voice PE) hardware does not use openWakeWord — it runs a separate on-device engine called microWakeWord.
systems.verification_note: Accuracy and footprint figures are the maintainer's own README claims, not independently re-verified. The Home Assistant OS add-on and ESPHome/Wyoming integration are independently confirmed via Home Assistant's own documentation and the home-assistant/addons repo — but that same documentation shows Home Assistant's Voice PE hardware runs a different engine (microWakeWord), not openWakeWord.

systems.name: microWakeWord
systems.method: Streaming inception-style CNN classifier over spectrogram features, quantized to int8 and run with TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers directly on the device chip (e.g. ESP32-S3) — inference every 30ms with no companion computer needed; models trained from synthetic Piper-TTS speech with SpecAugment.
systems.availability: Open source Python training framework, canonically maintained at OHF-Voice/micro-wake-word (originally developed by, and still actively co-developed on, Kevin Ahrendt's kahrendt/microWakeWord); pretrained .tflite models published separately at esphome/micro-wake-word-models; ships as the `micro_wake_word` component in ESPHome.
systems.best_for: On-chip wake word detection for ESP32-class microcontrollers where there is no host CPU at all — battery- or always-on embedded voice satellites (ESPHome / Home Assistant Voice hardware) that need the wake-word stage to run before anything else powers on.
systems.watch: The maintainer's own docs call this an 'early release' and warn that training a model which actually works well is still difficult and requires real hyperparameter experimentation — treat the bundled reference models as the safe path and budget real iteration time if you are training a genuinely new phrase yourself.
systems.standout: The only engine here designed to run entirely on the microcontroller with no host CPU at all: reference models fit in tens of kilobytes of tensor-arena RAM, and version 2 models now run on plain ESP32 chips (not just S3) with up to three wake words detected simultaneously.
systems.accuracy_note: No published false-accept/false-reject numbers were found in the docs reviewed; the runtime instead exposes a tunable probability-cutoff and sliding-window size so builders trade false-accepts against false-rejects themselves per deployment.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — open TensorFlow-based training pipeline using Piper-TTS synthetic speech, documented in the GitHub repo; described by the maintainer as usable but still advanced/early.
systems.footprint: Runs directly on ESP32-class microcontrollers; the example reference model ('okay nabu') uses a tensor arena as small as roughly 22.8 KB, per ESPHome's own component documentation.
systems.adoption: Ships as the on-device wake-word engine for Home Assistant Voice PE and is the default `micro_wake_word` component in ESPHome; also used for on-device detection in the Home Assistant Companion Android app.
systems.verification_note: Footprint and hardware claims are sourced from ESPHome's own component docs, independent of the training-repo README; no independently reproduced accuracy benchmark was found.

systems.name: OpenVoiceOS Precise (precise-lite / precise-onnx)
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (engine/plugin code); the pretrained-model repo (precise-lite-models) carries no declared licence on GitHub
systems.method: Per-wake-word RNN (GRU) classifier over MFCC audio features — the original Mycroft Precise architecture, kept alive and re-packaged by OpenVoiceOS first as 'precise-lite' (TensorFlow Lite runtime) and, since a November 2025 migration, re-exported to ONNX and served via onnxruntime as 'precise-onnx' to drop the aging tflite_runtime dependency.
systems.availability: Open source; installed as an OVOS/Mycroft wake-word plugin (`ovos-ww-plugin-precise-lite` or the newer `ovos-ww-plugin-precise-onnx`) with pretrained models pulled from OpenVoiceOS/precise-lite-models; trainer at OpenVoiceOS/precise-lite-trainer.
systems.best_for: Existing Mycroft/OpenVoiceOS/OVOS deployments that already use Precise-family wake words and want to keep them running as the underlying Python/ML dependency chain ages, without switching wake-word engines mid-fleet.
systems.watch: Two separate catches: (1) precise-lite, the TFLite runtime, isn't just end-of-life in spirit -- ovos-ww-plugin-precise-lite was formally archived (read-only) on GitHub as of Oct 31, 2025, and its own README still warns 'precise is no longer maintained, it is suggested you move to ovos-ww-plugin-precise-onnx' -- so new deployments should go straight to precise-onnx; and (2) the actual pretrained-model repository (OpenVoiceOS/precise-lite-models) carries no declared licence at all on GitHub (confirmed via the GitHub API: license is null), unlike the Apache-2.0 code around it, so shipping those specific model files commercially sits on shakier ground -- train your own via precise-lite-trainer if that matters for your use case.
systems.standout: A direct continuation of the original Mycroft AI wake-word engine after Mycroft's 2023 shutdown, so it carries years of real field deployment behind it (Mycroft Mark I/II hardware) rather than being a from-scratch project, including several already-trained non-English models (e.g. Spanish 'ey ordenador').
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — via the precise-lite-trainer tool, trained from your own recorded audio samples of the phrase (not synthetic TTS-generated, unlike openWakeWord/microWakeWord).
systems.footprint: OpenVoiceOS's own migration benchmark reports per-model CPU load on a Raspberry Pi 5 falling from roughly 1.8-2.6% (precise-lite/TFLite) to roughly 1.0-1.3% (precise-onnx) for the same wake-word models.
systems.adoption: Wake-word engine for the OpenVoiceOS/OVOS assistant stack (the community continuation of Mycroft AI) and historically the stock wake-word engine on Mycroft Mark I/II hardware.
systems.verification_note: CPU-load figures come from OpenVoiceOS's own blog post benchmarking their migration; precise-lite's end-of-life status and the models repo's licence field were both checked directly against OVOS's own README/GitHub metadata.

systems.name: WeKws
systems.method: End-to-end streaming keyword classifier trained with a max-pooling loss so the model learns the keyword's end position itself, avoiding a separate forced-alignment step; offers a choice of small-footprint backbones -- RNN/LSTM, TCN or its lightweight depthwise-separable variant (DS-TCN), and MDTC (multi-scale depthwise temporal convolution) -- exportable to on-device runtimes.
systems.availability: Open source (wenet-e2e/wekws on GitHub, from the WeNet speech-toolkit community); PyTorch for training, with shipped C++/ONNX Runtime deployment code for x86, Android, and Raspberry Pi. Web browser support is listed on the project's roadmap ('we plan to support... web browser') but has no runtime implementation in the repo yet.
systems.best_for: Teams comfortable training their own DNN-based keyword spotter who want a research-grade, actively-updated toolkit offering multiple backbone architectures to compare, rather than a single fixed pretrained model.
systems.watch: It is a training toolkit, not a batteries-included wake-word app — you supply or record your own keyword dataset (reference recipes cover public sets like Hey Snips, Google Speech Commands, and the Chinese Hi Xiaowen/Hi Mia corpora) and export/wire the runtime yourself; there is no synthetic-TTS-based one-click custom-phrase pipeline like openWakeWord or microWakeWord provide.
systems.standout: Built by the same WeNet community behind the widely-used WeNet ASR toolkit, backed by a companion peer-reviewed paper (ICASSP 2023) benchmarking multiple backbone architectures head-to-head, with commits as recent as July 2026 showing it is still actively developed rather than a one-off research drop.
systems.accuracy_note: The companion paper (Wang et al., 'WeKws: A production first small-footprint end-to-end Keyword Spotting Toolkit', arXiv:2210.16743 / ICASSP 2023) reports competitive results on Hey Snips, Google Speech Commands, and Hi Xiaowen benchmarks against prior KWS toolkits; figures are the authors' own and were not independently reproduced here.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes in principle — train any of the offered backbones on your own labeled keyword dataset — but there is no bundled synthetic-speech data-generation tool, so real or separately-sourced audio for the new phrase is required.
systems.verification_note: Accuracy claims trace to a peer-reviewed paper by the tool's own authors (ICASSP 2023); ongoing maintenance was independently confirmed via the repository's public commit history (commits through July 2026).

systems.name: SpeechBrain keyword-spotting recipe (Google Speech Commands)
systems.method: PyTorch training recipe, not a packaged detector: trains a closed-set classifier (an x-vector/TDNN model, or a LEAF-frontend variant) to label a fixed 12- or 35-word vocabulary from the Google Speech Commands dataset — output is a checkpoint, not a running wake-word listener.
systems.availability: Open source, part of the general-purpose SpeechBrain toolkit (speechbrain/speechbrain, recipes/Google-speech-commands); a pretrained x-vector checkpoint is also published on Hugging Face for direct inference without retraining.
systems.best_for: Researchers and ML engineers who want a well-documented PyTorch baseline for closed-vocabulary spoken-command classification, or a component to adapt inside a larger speech pipeline — not a drop-in 'listen for my phrase' wake-word engine.
systems.watch: This is fixed-vocabulary command CLASSIFICATION, not open-vocabulary wake-word SPOTTING: it labels a pre-segmented roughly-1-second clip as one of 12 or 35 known words and does not itself listen continuously to a live audio stream for an arbitrary custom phrase. Wiring in streaming/sliding-window detection, and choosing and recording a genuinely new wake phrase, is left to the builder.
systems.standout: The only entry here built on a general-purpose, broadly-used speech-ML toolkit (SpeechBrain) rather than a purpose-built wake-word project, so it inherits that ecosystem's documentation, Hugging-Face-hosted checkpoints, and PyTorch tooling — useful if you are already building a larger SpeechBrain-based pipeline.
systems.accuracy_note: SpeechBrain's own recipe reports 98.14% accuracy on the Google Speech Commands v12 test split with the x-vector model — a closed-set 12-word classification accuracy figure, not a wake-word false-accept/false-reject rate, so it is not directly comparable to the other rows here.
systems.custom_wake_word: Not out of the box — the shipped recipe classifies among Google Speech Commands' fixed word list; adapting it to an arbitrary new wake phrase means assembling your own labeled dataset and rewriting the recipe's data pipeline yourself, with no synthetic-data generator bundled.
systems.footprint: Not designed for embedded/MCU deployment like the other rows here — ships as a full PyTorch/Hugging Face model intended for server- or desktop-class inference.
systems.verification_note: Accuracy figure is SpeechBrain's own recipe README/model-card claim, not independently reproduced.

systems.name: Porcupine (Picovoice)
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (SDK/binding code); wake-word models are proprietary and require a Picovoice AccessKey
systems.price_note: A one-time, non-renewing Free Trial exists, but Picovoice's own FAQ states it is positioned for enterprise evaluation, not a standing non-commercial tier ("there are no dedicated free or paid plans for personal or non-commercial use"). All tiers are metered by Monthly Active Users (MAU) per engine (Porcupine/Rhino/Cobra), not by a count of custom wake words — no current Picovoice source supports a "3 wake words/month" cap. No public rate card was found; production/commercial use requires a paid Enterprise subscription arranged through sales, quote-based.
systems.method: On-device neural keyword spotting; compact trained models (under 1MB runtime, <25KB per keyword) run continuously on-CPU without a cloud round-trip
systems.availability: SDKs: Python, Node.js, Android, iOS, React/React Native/Flutter, .NET, Java, C, Web (WASM/browser)
systems.best_for: Cross-platform commercial products — from mobile apps down to Cortex-M microcontrollers — that need a fast, self-service custom wake word without recording or labeling training audio.
systems.watch: The SDK wrapper is Apache-2.0, but the wake-word models it loads are closed and gated behind a Picovoice AccessKey. Picovoice's current FAQ frames the Free Trial as enterprise evaluation, not a non-commercial hobbyist tier ("no dedicated free or paid plans for personal or non-commercial use"), and it is a one-time, non-renewing offer metered by Monthly Active Users per engine — not by a fixed number of custom wake words as sometimes cited. No public rate card exists; commercial deployment requires a quote-based paid Enterprise subscription via sales.
systems.standout: The self-service Picovoice Console trains a working custom wake word from typed text alone in seconds, with no recorded audio and no ML expertise required — most rivals in this list route custom phrases through a vendor engagement instead.
systems.accuracy_note: Picovoice's own benchmark reports 97.3% detection accuracy at 1 false alarm per 10 hours, and 97.1% accuracy at 10 dB SNR against background noise/competing speech; methodology is the vendor's own comparison suite, not an independent third-party test.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — self-service Picovoice Console trains a custom wake word from typed text in seconds (no audio recording, no ML expertise). Built-in languages: English, Mandarin, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish; other languages available case-by-case for commercial customers.
systems.footprint: Runtime under 1MB; individual compiled keyword files under 25KB each; vendor measured 0.6% CPU utilization on a Raspberry Pi 5.
systems.adoption: Picovoice states ~250K custom wake words were trained and deployed in 2025, citing enterprise customers including NASA, Adobe, Meta, Netflix, and Ferrari — vendor claim, not independently verified.
systems.verification_note: Licensing structure (Apache-2.0 SDK / proprietary models / AccessKey), SDK languages, and platform support are confirmed via Picovoice's official docs and public GitHub repo. The free-tier framing and unit of metering (Monthly Active Users, not wake-word count) are also confirmed via Picovoice's current FAQ, which contradicts an earlier, unverifiable "3 wake words/month, non-commercial" characterization of the free tier. Accuracy and adoption figures remain vendor-published and not independently verified.

systems.name: Sensory TrulyHandsfree
systems.licence: Proprietary — commercial SDK licence from Sensory Inc., terms negotiated per deployment (evaluation licences available for prototyping)
systems.price_note: Not published — proprietary licence negotiated per deployment/royalty; contact Sensory sales for pricing (free evaluation licence available for prototypes)
systems.method: On-device deep-neural-network keyword spotting; supports independent fixed wake words, user-enrolled fixed phrases, and fully user-defined wake words, plus optional voice-biometric speaker verification in the same pipeline
systems.availability: SDK for Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, QNX, Windows; licensed into automotive, mobile, consumer electronics, wearables, and robotics products
systems.best_for: OEMs (automotive, consumer electronics, wearables) needing an embedded wake-word engine with a long production track record, plus off-the-shelf models for major assistants (Alexa, Hey Siri, OK Google).
systems.watch: Pricing and licensing terms are not published anywhere in Sensory's own materials — every source on those points ends in 'contact Sensory.' Sensory's own wake-word product page does publish quantified relative false-reject-rate figures by noise condition against an unnamed competitor, so accuracy is not entirely unquantified; but no absolute FAR figures, and no disclosed identity for the competitor being compared against, are given — and the 2-billion-vs-3-billion adoption figure is inconsistent across Sensory's own pages.
systems.standout: Sensory's own materials cite a long production history — 'over 2 billion devices' per the cited product page, with other company materials claiming as many as 3 billion units and 200+ licensees (unreconciled across sources) — across automotive and consumer hardware that a newer SDK vendor cannot show, and the same engine doubles as an on-device speaker-verification system.
systems.accuracy_note: Sensory's own cited product page publishes comparative false-reject-rate figures for its current wake-word model against an unnamed competitor (0% FRR in silence vs. the competitor's 3%, 8% vs 15% in pink noise, 0% vs 10% in babble, 5% vs 13% in music); the competitor is not identified and no absolute FAR is given. Separately, Sensory states its newer deep-neural models deliver a 5x reduction in false accepts versus its own v4.01 baseline — a vendor-stated relative claim, not an independent benchmark.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — TrulyHandsfree supports independent fixed wake words, user-enrolled fixed phrases, and fully user-defined (builder-trained) wake words, alongside off-the-shelf models Sensory has offered for Alexa, Hey Siri (including globalized variants), OK Google, and several Asian cloud-assistant wake phrases. A previously offered 'Hey Cortana' model is no longer relevant: Microsoft retired the Cortana assistant in 2023.
systems.footprint: Historical spec: sound detector needs ~0.5 MIPS CPU, 1KB code memory, and a 10KB RAM audio-history buffer to initialize; the newer TrulyHandsfree 7.0 line claims model sizes down to 50KB and sub-1mW power. Individual wake-word models range roughly 20KB-2MB depending on the phrase.
systems.adoption: Sensory's own cited product page states 'over 2 billion devices powered by Sensory technology,' listing brands such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Samsung, Honda, Bentley, LG, Huawei, and Lenovo — a vendor claim, not independently verified. Other Sensory materials elsewhere claim 'over 200 licensees and over 3 billion products shipped,' a higher, unreconciled figure not found on this specific cited page.
systems.verification_note: Adoption, accuracy-improvement, and footprint figures are drawn from Sensory's own product pages, technical notes, and press releases; no independent third-party benchmark was found.

systems.name: Cyberon DSpotter / CSpotter
systems.licence: Proprietary — commercial licence from Cyberon Corporation, issued as chipset-tied licence files (free trial licence available)
systems.price_note: Not published — quote-based commercial licence from Cyberon or via silicon partners (Renesas, NXP, Infineon, XMOS); free trial license available, production licence files are issued per chipset ID
systems.method: Phoneme-based, speaker-independent neural keyword spotting for wake word plus local voice-command recognition; DSpotter targets MCU-class hardware, CSpotter adds on-device user-trained voice tags and speaker verification
systems.availability: Targets Arm Cortex-M MCUs and DSP/SoC platforms (CEVA, Tensilica, RISC-V via Andes); shipped through silicon-partner ecosystems including Renesas RA/RX, Infineon PSoC 6, NXP, GreenWaves, and XMOS xcore
systems.best_for: MCU and silicon vendors, and OEMs building wake word plus on-device voice commands into cost- and power-constrained embedded hardware, where new commands need to be authored from text rather than recorded speech.
systems.watch: Pricing and licence terms are not published anywhere — every source (Cyberon's own site and every silicon-partner page) routes to 'contact sales' for a quote, so cost cannot be compared up front, and no independently measured accuracy figure was found to check the qualitative 'high accuracy' claim against.
systems.standout: Wake words and voice commands are authored purely by typing the phrase into a phoneme-based acoustic model — no recorded training corpus is needed for a new command — and its published footprint (as low as ~200KB flash / ~24KB RAM, scaling with vocabulary) targets true microcontrollers rather than app processors.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — DSpotter/CSpotter wake words and voice commands are defined by typing the phrase (phoneme-based acoustic model), with no voice-data collection required for new commands; CSpotter additionally supports on-device user-trained voice tags and speaker verification. Vendor states 26+ languages supported, expanding roughly 4 languages/month.
systems.footprint: DSpotter: roughly 200KB + 42B-per-command flash and 24KB + 130B-per-command RAM, scaling with vocabulary size, per Renesas' partner documentation of the product.
systems.verification_note: Footprint numbers are sourced from Renesas' partner documentation of Cyberon's product; qualitative accuracy and noise-robustness claims are Cyberon's own marketing language and were not independently benchmarked. No adoption/unit figures were found to cite.

systems.name: SoundHound Wake Word
systems.licence: Proprietary — commercial licence as part of SoundHound's Voice AI / Houndify platform
systems.price_note: Not published — sold as a managed engagement within SoundHound's enterprise Voice AI offering (bespoke branded wake-word development); quote-based
systems.method: Bespoke on-device wake-word models built with deep neural networks, developed through a managed data-collection, labeling, and tuning engagement rather than a self-service trainer; runs locally to avoid cloud round-trip latency
systems.availability: SDKs for iOS, Android, C++, JavaScript, C#, Python, Java, Go, and React Native, as part of the broader Houndify/Voice AI platform (ASR, NLU, TTS, wake word)
systems.best_for: Brands that want a distinctive, trademarked wake phrase (their product name, not a generic 'Hey X') built into a voice product, with SoundHound handling ongoing tuning as part of a larger conversational-AI engagement.
systems.watch: This is a bespoke vendor-managed build, not a self-serve SDK — SoundHound states 'a few weeks' turnaround per custom wake word, so it does not fit a same-day integration the way a self-service trainer does, and no independent accuracy figures are published to check the marketing claim against.
systems.standout: Treats the wake word as brand IP (sonic branding) with ongoing production-data fine-tuning included, shipping as one piece of SoundHound's larger ASR/NLU/TTS stack rather than a standalone point tool — named production deployments include Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, and Motorola's 'Hello Moto' assistant.
systems.accuracy_note: SoundHound claims 'the most robust wake word models with highest response accuracy in the market' with no published FAR/FRR figures or test methodology — an unverifiable vendor claim.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — but delivered as a managed engagement (data collection, labeling, and post-launch tuning on production data) rather than self-service, typically a few weeks turnaround per vendor's stated timeline.
systems.adoption: SoundHound's own case studies name production users including Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, and Motorola's 'Hello Moto' assistant — vendor claim, not independently verified.
systems.verification_note: All capability, performance, and adoption claims are drawn from SoundHound's own product and case-study pages; no independent benchmark or third-party confirmation was found.
